title: Pauli Operators and Rotations
intro: The Pauli matrices are the observables, the generators of rotations, and (in tensor products) the basis for every operator on many qubits. A rotation of the Bloch sphere is the exponential of a Pauli, which is how inputs are written into qubits.

blocks.text: In the computational basis, $X$ swaps the two basis states ($X\vert0\rangle = \vert1\rangle$, $X\vert1\rangle = \vert0\rangle$), $Z$ flips the sign of $\vert1\rangle$ ($Z = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1)$), and $Y = iXZ$ does both with a phase ($Y\vert0\rangle = i\vert1\rangle$, $Y\vert1\rangle = -i\vert0\rangle$). As matrices, $X$ has rows $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, $Y$ has rows $(0, -i)$ and $(i, 0)$, and $Z$ has rows $(1, 0)$ and $(0, -1)$.
They are Hermitian (so they are observables, each with eigenvalues $\pm1$) and unitary (so they are also gates: $X$ is the quantum NOT). Their algebra is short enough to memorise:

items: Each squares to the identity: $X^2 = Y^2 = Z^2 = I$.
Distinct Paulis anticommute: $XY = -YX$, and so on.
Products cycle: $XY = iZ$, $YZ = iX$, $ZX = iY$. Hence $[X, Y] = 2iZ$ and its cyclic versions.
Together with $I$ they form a basis of all $2\times2$ matrices, orthogonal in the sense $\operatorname{Tr}(PQ) = 2\delta_{PQ}$.

blocks.text: The exponential of a Pauli is a rotation. Because $P^2 = I$, the power series splits into even and odd terms and closes into

blocks.caption: Rotation by angle θ about the axis of the Pauli P (P = X, Y or Z).

blocks.text: Acting on a state, $R_P(\theta)$ turns its Bloch vector by $\theta$ about the $P$ axis. The factor $1/2$ in the exponent is what makes a full turn $\theta = 2\pi$ give $-I$: the same physical state (a global phase), but a reminder that the state space double-covers the sphere. More generally, $e^{-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$ rotates about any unit axis $\hat n$, and every single-qubit unitary is such a rotation up to a phase.

Try it: the blue arrow is the starting state, the red one the state after the rotation, and the dashed arc the path between them. From $\vert0\rangle$, a 180° rotation about Y lands on $\vert1\rangle$, while 90° lands on $\vert+\rangle$. Rotating $\vert0\rangle$ about Z does nothing at all: the north pole is on the axis. To see the input encoding, keep the axis on Y and set the angle to $2\arcsin\sqrt s$ (for $s = 0.25$ that is 60°). Then put the start on the equator (θ = 90) and compare a 90° turn about X with one about Z.

Rotating about $x$ then $z$ is not the same as $z$ then $x$, for qubits as for books on a table. This is the commutator at work, and it is why the order of gates in a circuit matters and why a Hamiltonian $A + B$ with non-commuting parts cannot simply be split (Gates and Circuits (#/quantum/qubits/gates-and-circuits)).
Writing an input into a qubit

A rotation about $y$ from $\vert0\rangle$ stays on the real meridian: $R_Y(\theta)\vert0\rangle = \cos\frac\theta2\vert0\rangle + \sin\frac\theta2\vert1\rangle$. Choosing $\theta = 2\arcsin\sqrt s$ makes the $\vert1\rangle$ amplitude $\sqrt s$, which is the Fujii–Nakajima input state. Choosing $\theta = \pi s$ instead gives angle encoding, with $P(1) = \sin^2(\pi s/2)$. Same gate, different map from $s$ to angle, different function class for the reservoir (Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding)).

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1.]).astype(complex)
I = np.eye(2)
def R(P, theta): return expm(-1j * theta * P / 2)
# Closed form: R_P(theta) = cos(theta/2) I - i sin(theta/2) P for any Pauli P
print("closed form holds:", all(np.allclose(R(P, 0.8), np.cos(0.4) * I - 1j * np.sin(0.4) * P) for P in (X, Y, Z)))
# The QRC amplitude encoding: R_Y(2 arcsin sqrt(s))|0> = sqrt(1-s)|0> + sqrt(s)|1>
for s in (0.1, 0.25, 0.7):
    v = R(Y, 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(s))) @ np.array([1, 0])
    print(f"s = {s}: R_Y|0> = {np.round(v.real, 4)}, target {np.round([np.sqrt(1-s), np.sqrt(s)], 4)}")
# A 2 pi rotation gives -I: the global phase that spin-1/2 is famous for
print("R_Z(2 pi) = -I:", np.allclose(R(Z, 2 * np.pi), -I))
# Rotations about different axes do not commute
print("R_X(pi/2) R_Z(pi/2) == R_Z(pi/2) R_X(pi/2):", np.allclose(R(X, np.pi/2) @ R(Z, np.pi/2), R(Z, np.pi/2) @ R(X, np.pi/2)))
# Pauli algebra
print("XY = iZ:", np.allclose(X @ Y, 1j * Z), "  X^2 = I:", np.allclose(X @ X, I), "  {X, Z} = 0:", np.allclose(X @ Z + Z @ X, 0))

blocks.text: Output of the run: the closed form matches `expm` for all three axes; $R_Y(2\arcsin\sqrt s)\vert0\rangle$ reproduces $(\sqrt{1-s}, \sqrt s)$ for $s = 0.1, 0.25, 0.7$; $R_Z(2\pi) = -I$; $R_X(\pi/2)$ and $R_Z(\pi/2)$ do not commute; and $XY = iZ$, $X^2 = I$, $XZ + ZX = 0$ all hold.

blocks.title: A half turn
solution: $R_X(\pi) = -iX$, so $R_X(\pi)\vert0\rangle = -i\vert1\rangle$: the same state $\vert1\rangle$ up to a global phase.

blocks.title: Hadamard conjugation
blocks.text: The Hadamard $H_d = (X + Z)/\sqrt2$. Show that $H_dZH_d = X$.
solution: $H_dZH_d = (XZ + I)(X + Z)/2 = (XZX + XZZ + X + Z)/2 = (-Z + X + X + Z)/2 = X$, using $XZX = -Z$.
blocks.answer: H Z H = X (so measuring Z after H measures X)

blocks.title: Precessing an equatorial state
blocks.text: Apply $R_Z(\varphi)$ to $\vert+\rangle$. What is the Bloch vector, and which expectation values change?
solution: $R_Z(\varphi)$ turns the Bloch vector by $\varphi$ about $z$, so $(1, 0, 0) \to (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, 0)$.
$\langle X\rangle$ and $\langle Y\rangle$ change; $\langle Z\rangle = 0$ does not. A $Z$-only readout cannot see a $Z$ rotation.
